newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls broadly after overseas rally fizzles.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls broadly after overseas rally fizzles.

text.p: The dollar fell broadly on Thursday as a rally against the Japanese yen overseas fizzled and U.S. manufacturing data cast doubt over further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
Higher rates make yields on U.S. investments more attractive, boosting the value of the dollar.

The dollar rallied to a 56-month peak of 127.47 yen in Tokyo before sliding amid heavy selling by Japanese firms and on unconfirmed rumours that the Bank of Japan was intervening to prop up the ailing yen.

"A lot of the short-term and interbank traders were expecting a decent run-up once we broke above 127.15/30 yen and the fact of the matter is it didn't go much higher and the Japanese were heavy sellers," said David Gilmore, a partner at market consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"That has taken the wind out of the dollar's sail."

The dollar was dragged down further in U.S. trading on news that the National Association of Purchasing Management index fell to 54.2 in April from 55.0 in March, suggesting a slight slowdown in growth in manufacturing output.
The data reinforced the notion of a strong U.S. economy devoid of worrisome inflation, which was supported earlier this week by gross domestic product and labour cost data.

"Over the last couple of sessions, we've had numbers come out which suggested that perhaps the inflation component of the U.S. economy is not as high as the market had feared," said Audrey McNiff, a vice president in foreign exchange sales at Goldman Sachs & Co.
"This led the market to believe that the potential for interest rate rises is less than expected ... and it has taken some of the steam out of the dollar's movement."
Also, the Dow Jones industrial average slid 32.51 points to 6,976.48, a day after its furious rally over the 7,000 level, dampening enthusiasm about the dollar.

The dollar fell to 1.7225 German marks from 1.7311 at Wednesday's close and 126.58 yen from 127.13. Traders said business was thin during Japan's Golden Week holiday and as much of continental Europe was closed for May Day.
Speculation that President Bill Clinton and Congress were close to finalising a balanced budget accord supported the dollar.

Traders said a balanced budget pact would lift U.S. asset markets and benefit the dollar even though interest rates would likely fall amid requirements that the government tighten fiscal policy and issue less debt.
The dollar fell sharply against its Canadian counterpart, amid diminished prospects for a U.S. rate hike at the May 20 meeting of Fed policy-makers.

The Bank of Canada intervened twice in an attempt to cool off a rally in the Canadian dollar by purchasing U.S. dollars at C$1.3885 and then C$1.3870. The dollar closed more than one cent lower at C$1.3876 vs. C$1.3978 at Wednesday's close.
As Britons raced to the polls in the nation's parliamentary elections, the pound edged lower, in contrast to Wednesday's steep slide on pre-election jitters.
The pound inched lower to $1.6227 from $1.6240 Wednesday. In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4705 Swiss francs from 1.4735.
